title: Arc latency cohort + flame/heatmap notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from an exploratory session building an "arc"-style cohort view (heatmap + per-stage flame/stack) to understand e2e latency behavior across sequence length, kv-cache hit state, and batch sizes. Goal: identify high-impact mitigations for p99 regressions seen this week on the hosted text-gen route.

Key observations (summary):
- Baseline (route: text-gen-v2, default model quantized, 4xA10-like GPUs): p50=72ms, p95=250ms, p99=790ms for live traffic sample (N=150k requests / 24h).
- Cohort breakdown shows two dominant phenotypes for p99: long-seq CPU contention (seqlen>512) and unexpected kv-cache cold misses for medium sequences (seqlen 128-256) during microbursts.
- Per-stage flame analysis (tokenization -> input-prep -> kv-lookup -> model-kernel -> kv-write -> post-process -> egress) reveals model-kernel is dominant for seqlen>512 (~65–85% of time), but kv-lookup + preproc spikes account for 30–45% of p99 on 128–256 seqlen cohort during cold-cache windows.

Representative numbers (aggregated cohorts):
- Short (<=64 tokens): p50=48ms, p95=92ms, p99=210ms. Stage split (median p95 sample): tokenization 6ms, input-prep 8ms, kv-lookup 12ms, model-kernel 50ms, egress 6ms.
- Medium (128–256 tokens): p50=110ms, p95=280ms, p99=680ms. Stage split (p99 tail sample): tokenization 9ms, input-prep 15ms, kv-lookup 120ms (cold miss outliers 250ms), model-kernel 320ms, egress 16ms.
- Long (>512 tokens): p50=420ms, p95=820ms, p99=2.1s. Stage split (p99): tokenization 18ms, input-prep 40ms, kv-lookup 80ms, model-kernel 1600ms, egress 30ms.

Trace phenotypes found in flame/heatmap: 
1) Microburst-cold-kv: bursts of concurrent requests cause contention on the async KV client (JIT cache miss + single-threaded warm path). Manifest as clustered 100–300ms spikes in kv-lookup; shows high correlation with queue depth at batcher edge.
2) Kernel-swivel: long sequences trigger multiple kernel dispatches with suboptimal tiled kernels (fallback path). Flame shows many short kernel transitions and elevated GPU kernel launch overheads (~50–120ms per dispatch in worst cases).
3) Egress-saturation: rare but visible when responses are large (long sequences + streaming toggled); network egress latency adds 40–120ms variance, often correlated with simultaneous large downstream responses.

Hypotheses and quick checks performed:
- H1: KV client lock contention under bursts is primary driver for medium-seq p99s. Checked: thread profiling during spike windows shows serial access hotspot inside the cache-populate codepath.
- H2: Kernel selector falls back to generic kernels for >512 steps on the quantized model variant. Checked: runtime logs show selector reasons include unsupported attention kernel for combined rotary+grouped-qk layout.
- H3: Batching config (max-wait time) tuned aggressively for throughput increased queueing variance and made microbursts amplify kv-miss cost. Checked: synthetic replay with max-wait reduced from 10ms->3ms decreased p99 for medium cohort by ~18%.

Data sources and instrumentation used:
- Sampled traces (x-trace ids): set A (24h sample N=150k) + targeted replays via trace-replay tool with identical headers and controlled seqlen distribution.
- Stage timing metrics (per-request) from local telemetry pipeline and detailed CPU flame samples for worker process.
- GPU kernel traces from nvtx-annotated runs and kernel-level durations exported to Prometheus histogram.

Mitigations explored and short-term recommendations (ordered by expected impact):
1) KV-path parallelization: refactor cache-populate path to avoid global lock during cold miss (implement per-shard promise + background populate). Expect ~30–50% reduction in kv-lookup tail for medium cohort.
2) Batcher config change: lower max-wait from 10ms to 4ms for routes with median seqlen <256 and prioritize small requests via dynamic priority queue. Expected p99 improvement ~10–20% for mixed workloads. Rollout in canary.
3) Kernel selector patch: add explicit rule to prefer tiled GEMM for attention with grouped-qk when steps>256; add fallback telemetry. Medium-term (involves upstream kernel tuning).
4) Warm-start heuristic: pre-warm KV for identified heavy keys during load spikes (hot-prefix warming triggered by rate threshold). Low effort, medium impact.
5) Stream egress backpressure: for streaming-enabled clients, cap concurrent stream chunks per worker to avoid egress saturation; fallback to chunked-scheduling.

Operational playbook snippets (for on-call/triage):
- Detection: alert when p99 for medium cohort (128–256) rises >25% vs baseline AND kv-lookup p99 increases >50ms over baseline.
- Quick mitigation: temporarily reduce batcher max-wait for affected route to 2–4ms, enable warm-start of cache for top-N hot keys (via admin API).
- Deep triage: collect CPU flame + nvtx kernel traces across 1–2 minute window, annotate with batcher queue depth histogram, and run trace-replay to reproduce.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Need to quantify impact of shard count for kv-cache on tail. Hypothesis: more shards => lower contention but higher memory overhead; run A/B with 4 vs 16 shards.
- Evaluate cost tradeoffs for warm-start warming (extra remote reads vs latency saved). Add to Optimize cost model.
- Confirm whether grouped-qk kernels can be avoided by small model-rewrite or if kernel team can provide optimized kernels for our quant path.

Action items (owners):
- Rafael: prototype per-shard promise cache-populate (P0), timeline 2 weeks.
- Priya: small canary for batcher max-wait tweak + dynamic priority queue (P0), deploy canary tomorrow, monitor 48h.
- Jonas: collect targeted nvtx traces for >512 seqlen runs and file kernel selector bug with kernel team (P1).
- Maya: bake these cohort definitions into the daily latency-scan job and add the medium-cohort p99 alert (P0).

Notes on uniqueness of arc view:
- The "arc" view maps two axes: x=seqlen bins, y=batch-size/kv-hit state, cell color=p95 or p99; each cell links to a lightweight flamegraph (svg) summarizing stage percentages. This made it much faster to scan which seqlen vs state combos drive the end-to-end tail vs simply looking at global p99.
- Implementation idea: store per-cohort micro-aggregates (histograms + top-3 stage contributors) so the UI can render cell-level flames without heavy trace sampling on-demand.

Appendix (example trace snippets):
- Example p99 medium-seq trace id: x-trace-20251112-01 -> timeline: tokenization 8ms | input-prep 14ms | kv-lookup 270ms (cold-miss; 3x remote reads serialized) | model-kernel 320ms | kv-write 12ms | egress 10ms | total 634ms.
- Example p99 long-seq trace id: x-trace-20251112-02 -> timeline: tokenization 22ms | input-prep 36ms | kv-lookup 62ms | model-kernel 1.95s (multiple kernel dispatch overheads) | egress 18ms | total 2.09s.

I want to convert this draft into an internal playbook entry and a short one-pager for the SRE runbook once we validate the per-shard cache change in staging. Keeping notes here so we can iterate quickly.

-- Maya
